adults.title: While We Wait for Deliverance
adults.big_idea: Jesus Christ will deliver the righteous from every affliction in His time and way, and while we wait He visits us with assurances and with grace that enables us to endure.
adults.objective: Learners will be able to describe the pattern of divine deliverance Elder Hathaway taught, recognize where they are in it now, and choose one way to turn toward the Savior this week.
prepare: Read the talk once, marking the four parts of the pattern in the paragraph that follows the freeway story.

Write the four parts on the board before class: 1. Opposition brings questions and emotions. 2. Sincere seeking invites assurances. 3. Christ's grace enables us to endure and grow. 4. Deliverance comes in His time and way.
Bring a small card or slip of paper and a pen for each person.
Write the four group assignments from the third segment on slips of paper.
Pray for those in your class who are waiting on the Lord right now. You may not know who they are.

segments.name: A burden no one else can see
steps: After the prayer, slowly read the question Elder Hathaway asked at the start of his talk: have we ever felt left out, wondered if we were enough, lost someone we loved, faced illness, experienced family difficulties, or carried a burden no one else could see?
Give each person a card. Allow one quiet minute to write one burden they are carrying or waiting on. Say clearly that no one will see the card or be asked to share it.
Ask the question below and take two or three brief answers.
Read the first key quote, which begins “His deliverance is certain.” Say that today's lesson is about the how and the when.
questions: Without naming the burden, what is the hardest part of waiting for the Lord's help?

segments.name: A pattern on the roadside
steps: Retell the freeway story briefly and faithfully: the Hathaways were driving in two cars to begin their service as mission leaders when two large tires came loose from a semitruck in a construction zone and struck both cars at high speed. The airbags deployed, the cars were destroyed, and the family stood stranded on the roadside wondering why this had happened when they had left everything to serve the Lord.

Tell what came next: in that moment the Spirit brought them peace that everything would be all right. They were not immediately delivered, but the assurance gave them hope. With the help of many wonderful people they arrived on time and began their mission without serious injury.
Point to the four parts on the board and read the second key quote, which states the pattern in Elder Hathaway's words.
Ask the question below. Help the class notice that the assurance came before the problem was solved.
questions: Which parts of the pattern can you see in this story, and in what order did they come?

segments.name: Search the pattern in scripture
steps: Divide into four groups (or four pairs). Give each group one slip.

Group 1, opposition and questions: D&C 121:1–8. Group 2, sincere seeking and assurances: Mosiah 24:10–16. Group 3, enabled enduring: D&C 123:17 with Alma 7:11–12. Group 4, deliverance in His time: Mark 5:35–42.
Ask every group to read and prepare a one-sentence answer to the two questions below.
Walk among the groups. Give a one-minute warning before time is up.
questions: What did the people in these verses feel or do in their affliction?
What did the Lord give them before the affliction was over?

segments.name: Report, then hear Sister Brinkerhoff
steps: Invite each group to give its one-sentence report, in order, so the class hears the whole pattern. Keep each report under a minute.

Tell the account of Sister Kenzie Brinkerhoff with care. On the last preparation day before she returned home from her mission, her father, Kelly, called early in the morning to tell her he loved her, was proud of her, and was excited to hug her soon. That night, driving home from work, he was in a vehicle accident and passed away. When Elder and Sister Hathaway arrived, she asked through her tears how this could happen when she was one week from hugging her dad.
Read the third key quote, her words to Elder Hathaway several weeks later. Pause before you ask the questions.
Point out what Elder Hathaway taught about such questions and emotions: they are not sin or weakness. They can be a sacred space where we choose whether to turn toward Jesus Christ.
questions: How can the same weeks be both “most awful” and “most sacred”?
When has holding to your covenants helped you endure something you could not carry alone? Share only what you are comfortable sharing.

segments.name: When the hour seems too late
steps: Read the fourth key quote, which begins “the Lord is not delayed.”
Read Elder Kearon's words that Elder Hathaway quoted (see aligned quotes), then the words of Elder Chigbundu from this conference.

Explain that Elder Hathaway taught that grace does not remove the pain and difficulty of affliction. It is an enabling power. He also taught that some miracles are immediate, some come after long waiting, and some await the Resurrection.
Ask the question below. Let silence do its work before anyone answers.
questions: What have you learned while waiting that an earlier rescue might not have taught you?

segments.name: Choose one way to turn toward Him
steps: Ask learners to look again at their card and silently write which part of the pattern they are in right now.

Remind them how Elder Hathaway described sincere seeking: heartfelt prayer, purposeful fasting, and scripture study. Invite them to write one of these they will do this week for the burden on the card.

Share the promise taught in the talk: as we humbly and patiently keep our covenants, the Savior will visit us in our afflictions and bring assurances of deliverance. Bear your own brief testimony that Jesus Christ is the Great Deliverer.
Follow up next week: begin by asking what assurance class members noticed this week. Be ready to share one of your own first.

key_quotes.text: His deliverance is certain; the question for most righteous followers is not if He will deliver but how and when He will do so.
Opposition brings heartrending questions and emotions, sincere seeking invites assurances, Christ’s grace enables us to endure and grow, and deliverance comes in the Savior’s time and way.
The past few weeks have been the most awful and the most sacred time in my life. I have never clung so tightly to my covenants. I know that Jesus knows what this feels like, and He will heal me.

the Lord is not delayed, distracted, or derelict in His deliverance. He has not forgotten you. He does not take joy in your suffering. However, He knows that lessons learned while waiting can bring converting growth that an earlier rescue might not produce.

scriptures.use: Group 1 reads it. Look for Joseph Smith's questions in the first verses and the Lord's assurance in verses 7–8, given while he was still in Liberty Jail.
Group 2 reads it. Mark what Alma's people did in bondage and what the Lord gave them before He led them out.
Group 3 reads it with Alma 7:11–12. Find the two things we are asked to do, then discuss how the Savior's grace makes the first one possible.
Group 4 reads it. Notice the moment Jairus hears it is too late and what Jesus says to him next.

aligned_quotes.text: Jesus specializes in the seemingly impossible. He came here to make the impossible possible, the irredeemable redeemable, to heal the unhealable, to right the unrightable, to promise the unpromisable. And He’s really good at it. In fact, He’s perfect at it.
aligned_quotes.speaker: Elder Patrick Kearon
Elder Chigbundu
aligned_quotes.text: The burden we carry may not always be removed, but our backs will be built to carry the load placed upon them

takeaways: The Savior's deliverance is certain; the open questions are how and when.
Hard questions and deep feelings are not sin or weakness. They are a moment to turn toward Jesus Christ.
While we wait, He sends assurances and grace that help us endure and grow.
act: Keep your card where you pray. Each day this week, tell Heavenly Father honestly about that one burden and then listen for a moment.
Choose one act of sincere seeking for the week: a heartfelt prayer at a set time, a purposeful fast, or a daily reading of Mosiah 24:10–16.
Write down any assurance of peace, faith, or hope that comes, with the date, so you can remember it later.
Think of someone who is waiting on the Lord. Reach out this week simply to listen.
adapt: At home or with a very small group: skip the groups. Read Mosiah 24:10–16 and Mark 5:35–36 together and answer the two search questions as you go.
Large class: use eight groups, two for each passage, and take one report per passage.
Short on time: keep the card, the freeway story, Sister Brinkerhoff's words, and the closing choice. Assign the scripture passages as study for the week.

youth.title: Not If, but How and When
youth.big_idea: Hard questions are not sin or weakness; they are a moment to choose to turn toward Jesus Christ, who will deliver us in His time and way.
youth.objective: Youth will be able to explain the four-part pattern of deliverance in Elder Hathaway's talk and choose one specific way to turn toward the Savior the next time something hard happens.
prepare: Read the talk, especially the story of Sister Brinkerhoff, so you can tell it gently in your own words.
Bring slips of paper, pens, and a cup or bowl.

For each team of two or three, write the four parts of the pattern on four separate strips and mix them up: Opposition brings heartrending questions and emotions / Sincere seeking invites assurances / Christ's grace enables us to endure and grow / Deliverance comes in the Savior's time and way.
Ask youth to have their scriptures or the Gospel Library app ready.
If someone in your class is grieving, do not call on them by name during this lesson. Let every personal comment be volunteered.

segments.name: The question cup
steps: As youth come in, hand each a slip. Ask them to finish this sentence without writing a name: A question someone my age might ask God when life gets hard is…
Collect the slips in the cup. After the prayer, read four or five aloud without comment.
Take a quick vote with thumbs up, sideways, or down on the question below. Do not settle it yet.
questions: Is it all right for a faithful person to ask God questions like these?

segments.name: Questions are not sin
steps: Race: who can find D&C 121:1 first? Have the winner read it aloud and tell who asked it and where he was (Joseph Smith, in Liberty Jail).
Read the first key quote, which begins “Such questions and emotions.” Ask a youth to say it back in their own words.
Share Sister Runia's sentence from this conference (see aligned quotes).
In pairs, give one minute for the first question below. Then hear from two or three pairs.
questions: What does turning toward Jesus Christ with a hard question look like? What does turning away look like?
Why do you think Elder Hathaway called that moment a sacred space?

segments.name: Pattern scramble
steps: Put youth in teams of two or three. Give each team a set of mixed-up strips. The first team to put the four parts in the right order wins. Check against the second key quote.

Tell the freeway story: the Hathaway family was driving in two cars to begin serving as mission leaders. In a construction zone two large tires came loose from a semitruck and struck both cars at high speed. The airbags deployed and the cars were destroyed. They stood on the roadside wondering why this had happened when they had left everything to serve the Lord. Then the Spirit brought them peace that everything would be all right. With the help of many wonderful people, they arrived on time and began their mission without serious injury.
Round two: each team lays its strips in a row and decides which moment of the story fits each one. Ask one team to explain its matches.
Point out one detail: they were not delivered right away. The peace came first.
questions: Why might the Lord send peace before He sends the solution?

segments.name: Most awful and most sacred
steps: Say that the next account is tender. Tell it simply: Sister Kenzie Brinkerhoff was a missionary one week from going home. On her last preparation day her dad called early in the morning to say he loved her, was proud of her, and was excited to hug her soon. That night he was in a vehicle accident on his way home from work and passed away. When Elder and Sister Hathaway came to her, she asked through her tears how this could happen when she was a week from hugging her dad.
Ask where her question fits in the pattern on the strips.
Invite a youth to read the third key quote: what Sister Brinkerhoff said several weeks later.
Have everyone open Alma 7:11–12 and silently find two things: what the Savior took upon Himself, and why. Hear answers, then ask the questions below.
questions: Sister Brinkerhoff said she knows that Jesus knows what this feels like. How does Alma 7:11–12 back that up?
She did not say the pain was gone. What had changed?

segments.name: When it feels too late
steps: Read Mark 5:35–36 together. Ask what message Jairus had just received and what Jesus said to him.
Read Elder Kearon's words that Elder Hathaway quoted (see aligned quotes), then the fourth key quote about three kinds of timing for miracles.

Create: in the same teams, write a short message of two or three sentences you could send to a friend who has been praying about something for a long time and is tired of waiting. Use one idea from today. Be honest, not cheesy.
Ask one or two teams to read theirs aloud.
questions: Which is hardest to trust: a miracle that is immediate, one that comes after long waiting, or one that awaits the Resurrection? Why?

segments.name: My turn-toward plan
steps: Return to the opening vote and ask if anyone would answer differently now.

Remind the class how Elder Hathaway described sincere seeking: heartfelt prayer, purposeful fasting, and scripture study. Ask each youth to open a note on their phone or a slip of paper and write: The next time something hard happens, the first thing I will do is…

Share the promise taught in the talk: as we humbly and patiently keep our covenants, the Savior will visit us in our afflictions and bring assurances of deliverance. Add your own short testimony of Jesus Christ.
Follow up next week: start class by asking who used their plan and what they noticed. Share your own experience first.

key_quotes.text: Such questions and emotions are not sin or weakness; they can create a sacred space where agency is activated and we choose whether to turn toward Jesus Christ.
Opposition brings heartrending questions and emotions, sincere seeking invites assurances, Christ’s grace enables us to endure and grow, and deliverance comes in the Savior’s time and way.
The past few weeks have been the most awful and the most sacred time in my life. I have never clung so tightly to my covenants. I know that Jesus knows what this feels like, and He will heal me.
In His time and way, Jesus Christ will deliver you. Some miracles are immediate, some come after long waiting, and some await the Resurrection.

scriptures.use: Race to find it. Read it aloud and name who asked this question and where. Use it to show that prophets have asked hard questions too.
Read silently on phones or in scriptures. Find what the Savior took upon Himself and the reason given in verse 12.
Read together. Identify the bad news Jairus received and the Savior's five-word answer, which Elder Hathaway repeated to all who face pain, fear, and loneliness.

aligned_quotes.speaker: Sister Runia
aligned_quotes.text: Not understanding is not the same as not believing.

Jesus specializes in the seemingly impossible. He came here to make the impossible possible, the irredeemable redeemable, to heal the unhealable, to right the unrightable, to promise the unpromisable. And He’s really good at it. In fact, He’s perfect at it.
aligned_quotes.speaker: Elder Patrick Kearon

takeaways: Asking God hard questions is not sin or weakness.
Jesus Christ knows what my pain feels like, and He knows how to help me.
He will deliver me in His time and way, and He sends peace while I wait.
act: Take one honest question to Heavenly Father in prayer this week. Say it out loud if you can, then stay on your knees for one quiet minute.
Read Alma 7:11–12 each night for a week and note one word that stands out each time.
Send the message your team wrote, in your own words, to someone who is having a hard time.
The next time something goes wrong, try your turn-toward plan first, before anything else.
music: Where Can I Turn for Peace?
adapt: At home or with one or two youth: skip the competition. Lay out the four strips together and match them to the freeway story as a family.
Large class: run the scramble as boys against girls or by rows, and collect the written messages to read a few aloud.
Short on time: keep the question cup, the first key quote, Sister Brinkerhoff's words with Alma 7:11–12, and the closing plan.

children.title: Jesus Helps Me When Things Are Hard
children.big_idea: Jesus Christ helps me when things are hard.
children.objective: Children will be able to say that Jesus Christ helps them when things are hard and will choose to pray the next time they feel sad or afraid.
prepare: Read the freeway story near the beginning of Elder Hathaway's talk so you can tell it simply.
Bring a bag or backpack with three or four books in it. It should be heavy enough to notice but safe for a child to lift.
Bring a flashlight, plain paper, and crayons.
Write on the board or a paper: Jesus Christ helps me when things are hard.
Set chairs in two short rows to be two cars.

segments.name: Sing and say
steps: Sing the first verse of “A Child's Prayer” together and invite a child to pray.
Teach today's truth with actions: Jesus Christ (hand on heart) helps me (hug yourself) when things are hard (push both hands forward as if pushing something heavy).
Say it together three times: loud, soft, then in a whisper.

segments.name: The heavy bag
steps: Set the bag of books on the floor. Let a few children take turns carrying it across the room alone. Ask how it felt.
Now carry it with each child, both holding the handle. Ask the first question below.

Tell them that in the Book of Mormon, Alma's people had very hard things to carry. They prayed to God with all their hearts, and the Lord made them strong so their burdens felt light. Later He led them to freedom. Show the children where this is in Mosiah 24:14–15.
Explain: Sometimes Jesus takes the hard thing away. Sometimes He makes us strong enough to carry it. Either way, He helps. Say the truth together with the actions.
questions: What changed when someone helped you carry the bag?
Who can help us with hard things that no one else can see?

segments.name: Act out the story
steps: Seat the children in the two rows of chairs. Say: Elder Hathaway and his family were driving in two cars to begin serving a mission. Let the children hold pretend steering wheels and drive.
Say: Suddenly two big tires came off a truck and hit their cars. The cars were broken and could not go anymore. Have the children stop, climb out, and stand by the side of the road.
Ask how the family might have felt. Let children show the feeling on their faces. Say that they wondered why this had happened when they were going to serve the Lord.

Say: Right then, the Holy Ghost gave them peace. They felt that everything would be all right. Invite the children to put a hand on their heart, take a slow breath, and whisper, “Everything would be all right.”
Finish the story: Many kind people helped them. No one was badly hurt, and they got to their mission on time. Have the children climb back in and drive on, waving thank you to the helpers.
Ask the questions below, then say the truth together.
questions: What did the family feel in their hearts before their problem was fixed?

segments.name: Be not afraid
steps: Tell the children that once a father named Jairus was very worried about his daughter. Jesus said to him, “Be not afraid, only believe.” Jairus believed, and Jesus helped his family.
Practice the words together. You say, “Be not afraid,” and the children answer, “only believe.”

Play a walking game. The children walk quietly around the room. When you say, “Be not afraid,” they freeze, put a hand on their heart, and answer, “only believe.” Play four or five rounds, changing how they move each time: tiptoe, giant steps, slow motion.
Sit down together and ask the question below.
questions: When might you want to remember these words of Jesus?

segments.name: Draw it
steps: Give each child a paper folded in half and some crayons.
On one half, invite them to draw something that can feel hard for a child, such as being afraid of the dark, feeling left out, or being sick.
On the other half, invite them to draw themselves praying or Jesus helping them.
While they draw, move from child to child and ask them to tell you about their picture. Write today's truth at the top of each paper, or let older children write it themselves.

segments.name: Pass the light
steps: Gather the children in a circle and turn on the flashlight. Say that the peace the Holy Ghost brings is like a light that tells us Jesus is helping us, even while we wait.
Pass the flashlight around the circle. Each child who holds it finishes this sentence: When something is hard, I can…
Accept every sincere answer, such as pray, ask for help, or remember Jesus. Help the youngest by whispering an idea.

segments.name: Choose and close
steps: Read Elder Lebethoa's words from this conference (see aligned quotes) and tell the children in one or two sentences how you know Jesus Christ helps us.
Invite each child to choose: This week, when something feels hard, I will say a prayer. Ask them to show the drawing to someone at home and tell what they chose.
Say the truth one last time with the actions, and close with prayer.
Follow up next week: begin by asking who prayed when something was hard and what happened.

key_quotes.text: Jesus Christ is the Great Deliverer!
the Spirit brought us peace: Everything would be all right.
In His time and way, Jesus Christ will deliver you.

scriptures.use: After the heavy bag activity, show the children where this is in the Book of Mormon and tell in your own words how the Lord helped Alma's people. Older children can read verse 15 aloud.
Use for the walking game. The Savior's words in this verse are quoted in the talk, so the children can repeat them. An older child can find and read the verse first.

aligned_quotes.speaker: Elder Lebethoa
aligned_quotes.text: Whatever concerns, challenges, and struggles we may have in our lives, the answer is always Jesus Christ.

takeaways: Jesus Christ helps me when things are hard.
When I am sad or afraid, I can pray.
The Holy Ghost can help me feel peace.
act: Pray to Heavenly Father when something feels hard this week.
Show your drawing to someone at home and teach them the truth with the actions.
Be a helper: notice someone carrying something heavy or having a hard day, and offer to help.

adapt.younger: Ages 3–7: keep each part short and repeat the truth with actions after every activity. Carry the bag with every child, since each will want a turn. In the story, give simple directions one at a time (drive, stop, hand on heart). For the drawing, let them draw only themselves praying, and have a helper write the words. Explain that deliver means to rescue or help.
adapt.older: Ages 8–11: invite a child to read Mosiah 24:15 and another to read Mark 5:36 aloud. Let an older child lead the walking game and narrate part of the story. Ask a harder question: Why might Jesus give us peace first and fix the problem later? Have them write on their drawing one thing they will do the next time something is hard.
